preamble: The shift from the voiced velar stop [g] to the voiceless velar fricative [x] involves two phonetic processes: spirantization (weakening from a stop to a fricative) and devoicing. This shift is a defining characteristic of West Germanic languages, particularly Dutch and dialects of German.

examples.from: PIE *k before consonant (yielding *g in voiced clusters)
examples.note: Proto-Iranian spirantization of velar stops in consonant clusters: *g-clusters → *ɣ/x. Cf. Avestan xšāθra- 'realm' and xvara- forms where cluster-initial velars surface as fricatives. The process parallels Germanic consonant shift but applies specifically to pre-consonantal environments.

Northwestern Songhay variety Tadaksahak has developed a series of velar fricatives including [ɣ] and [x] through contact with Tuareg (Berber) and internal lenition processes. Inherited and borrowed voiced velars [g] surface as spirantized [ɣ] in intervocalic positions, paralleling the Berber substrate influence on this Nilo-Saharan variety. This is partly areal and partly inherited Songhay phonological tendency toward velar weakening.

Kabyle spirantization: lax /g/ in intervocalic and post-vocalic positions weakens to the voiced velar fricative [ɣ]. The reflex is voiced [ɣ] (not devoiced [x]); geminate /gg/ resists spirantization and surfaces as a stop. Kabyle is a prototypical 'spirantizing' Berber language.

Central and northern Moroccan Berber dialects spirantize lax /g/ to [ɣ] in intervocalic environments. The palatalization variant [ʝ] or [j] occurs before front vowels in some dialects. Spirantization is absent in southern (High Atlas) Tamazight dialects.

sources: Windfuhr, G. (Ed.). (2009). The Iranian Languages. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203641736
